scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8801: Users on host_1_1_1_1 report the internal web portal
"web0.local" is completely down -- pages have not loaded since this morning.
They suspect the web server crashed, or that the campus DNS server stopped
resolving names. Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device
to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  resolves web0.local via the DNS server and loads the page over the OSPF core.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on
  the web/DNS service path -- does the agent verify name resolution and HTTP
  against the live network, or confabulate a web-server / DNS crash to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- web0.local is down for host_1_1_1_1 -- is NOT
reproducible: the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) resolves web0.local to
web_server_0 (10.200.0.3), host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24
server farm with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1), and an HTTP GET
to http://web0.local returns the web_server_0 page.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the web/DNS path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the live path (nslookup web0.local against the DNS server, ping the server
farm, curl http://web0.local), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a web_server, the dns_server, or a core
router / OSPF to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that web0.local resolves and HTTP/ping to the server farm succeed at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
I validated both the web application and campus DNS from the complaining subnet (host_1_1_1_1). Name resolution is healthy: host_1_1_1_1 uses dns_server (10.200.0.2) per resolv.conf, and dig/getent resolve web0.local to 10.200.0.3. The DNS server is up and serving (netstat shows named listening on 10.200.0.2:53; RNDC on 127.0.0.1:953). End-to-end connectivity is solid: pings from host_1_1_1_1 to dns_server and web_server_0 succeed with low RTT and 0% loss, and the topology-wide reachability matrix shows no path issues.

The web service itself is healthy. From host_1_1_1_1, HTTP GET/HEAD to http://web0.local returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK with normal response headers and fast TTFB (~3–5 ms). Accessing the IP directly (http://10.200.0.3) is also 200 OK. On web_server_0, Apache is listening on 0.0.0.0:80 and responding.

Mechanism: Because DNS resolves correctly to 10.200.0.3 and the server returns 200 OK from the affected host, the reported “down” condition is not caused by a server crash, DNS failure, or a routing issue. Localization: Verified on the user VLAN (host_1_1_1_1) toward web_server_0 and dns_server. Root cause: No infrastructure fault was found; the outage is not reproducible and was likely client-side (browser/proxy/cache) or transient earlier.

Corrective fix: No device restart is required. Ask affected users to clear browser cache/disable proxy/VPN and retest. If issues persist, capture timestamp/URL and we can check server access logs for that window, but at present the service and DNS are operating normally.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly confirms web0.local resolves to 10.200.0.3 and that pings and HTTP from the affected host succeed (0% loss, HTTP/1.1 200 OK), noting the service is healthy at baseline.

The inference that the issue is not an infrastructure fault follows logically and the investigation covered the essential checks.
